items.stem: What is an ionic bond?
options: the attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
a shared pair of electrons between two atoms
the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
items.answer: the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
items.markingKey: Ionic bond: electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions.

items.stem: Explain why sodium forms an Na⁺ ion and not an Na²⁺ ion.
items.answer: Sodium (2,8,1) loses its single outer electron to reach the stable configuration 2,8 of neon; removing a second electron from a full shell would need far more energy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: loses one outer electron; 1 mark: achieves full outer shell / noble gas configuration [2]

items.stem: Explain why the formula of calcium chloride is CaCl₂.
items.answer: Calcium loses two electrons to form Ca²⁺; each chlorine atom gains only one electron to form Cl⁻, so two chloride ions are needed to balance the charge of one calcium ion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻; 1 mark: charges balance 2 × (1−) [2]

items.stem: Chloe, a student in Singapore, burns potassium in oxygen to make potassium oxide. Describe how the ions form, in terms of electron transfer.
items.answer: Each potassium atom (2,8,8,1) loses 1 outer electron to form K⁺ (2,8,8); each oxygen atom (2,6) gains 2 electrons to form O²⁻ (2,8). 2 potassium atoms transfer electrons to 1 oxygen atom, and the oppositely charged ions attract (ionic bond), giving K₂O.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: potassium loses 1 electron(s); 1 mark: oxygen gains 2 electron(s); 1 mark: ions K⁺ and O²⁻ [3]

items.stem: Amara, a student in Madrid, burns sodium in oxygen to make sodium oxide. Describe how the ions form, in terms of electron transfer. Include the electronic configurations of the atoms and ions (proton numbers: sodium 11, oxygen 8).
items.answer: Each sodium atom (2,8,1) loses 1 outer electron to form Na⁺ (2,8); each oxygen atom (2,6) gains 2 electrons to form O²⁻ (2,8). 2 sodium atoms transfer electrons to 1 oxygen atom, and the oppositely charged ions attract (ionic bond), giving Na₂O.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sodium loses 1 electron(s); 1 mark: oxygen gains 2 electron(s); 1 mark: ions Na⁺ and O²⁻; 1 mark: configurations 2,8,1 → 2,8 and 2,6 → 2,8 [4]

items.stem: Describe, in terms of electrons, how lithium fluoride forms when lithium reacts with fluorine. Include the electronic configurations of the atoms and ions (proton numbers: lithium 3, fluorine 9). Describe the dot-and-cross diagram for the compound and deduce its formula.
items.answer: Each lithium atom (2,1) loses 1 outer electron to form Li⁺ (2); each fluorine atom (2,7) gains 1 electron to form F⁻ (2,8). and the oppositely charged ions attract (ionic bond), giving LiF.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lithium loses 1 electron(s); 1 mark: fluorine gains 1 electron(s); 1 mark: ions Li⁺ and F⁻; 1 mark: configurations 2,1 → 2 and 2,7 → 2,8; 1 mark: diagram shows 1 × [lithium ion]¹⁺ and 1 × [fluorine ion] with 8 outer electrons and charge 1−; 1 mark: formula LiF [6]

items.stem: Calcium oxide is an ionic compound formed from calcium (proton number 20) and oxygen (proton number 8). A research group in Mexico City is studying its structure. (a) Give the electronic configurations of both atoms. (b) Describe how the ions are formed.
items.answer: (a) 2,8,8,2; 2,6 (b) calcium loses 2 electron(s) to form Ca²⁺; oxygen gains 2 to form O²⁻.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each ion with electrons lost/gained [2]

items.stem: Lithium fluoride is an ionic compound formed from lithium (proton number 3) and fluorine (proton number 9). A research group in Hanoi is studying its structure. (a) Give the electronic configurations of both atoms. (b) Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of the compound, showing outer shells only.
items.answer: (a) 2,1; 2,7 (b) 1 Li⁺ ion(s) with empty/full outer shell and 1 F⁻ ion(s) each with 8 outer electrons (including 1 of the other symbol); brackets and charges.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: correct number of each ion; 1 mark: 8 electrons on anion with transferred electrons shown; 1 mark: charges [3]

items.stem: What happens to the electrons when magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide?
options: Each magnesium atom transfers one electron to an oxygen atom.
Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to an oxygen atom.
Magnesium and oxygen share two pairs of electrons.
Each oxygen atom transfers two electrons to a magnesium atom.
items.answer: Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to an oxygen atom.

items.stem: Describe what a dot-and-cross diagram for sodium chloride shows.
items.answer: Na⁺ with a full outer shell (or no outer electrons shown) and Cl⁻ with eight outer electrons, seven of one symbol and one of the other showing the transferred electron; both ions in brackets with their charges.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Na⁺ shell; 1 mark: Cl⁻ with 8 including the transferred electron; 1 mark: charges [3]

items.stem: Describe, in terms of electrons, how sodium oxide forms when sodium reacts with oxygen.
items.answer: Each sodium atom (2,8,1) loses 1 outer electron to form Na⁺ (2,8); each oxygen atom (2,6) gains 2 electrons to form O²⁻ (2,8). 2 sodium atoms transfer electrons to 1 oxygen atom, and the oppositely charged ions attract (ionic bond), giving Na₂O.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sodium loses 1 electron(s); 1 mark: oxygen gains 2 electron(s); 1 mark: ions Na⁺ and O²⁻ [3]

items.stem: Noah heats lithium (proton number 3) in nitrogen (proton number 7). A white solid, lithium nitride, is formed. (a) Give the electronic configurations of both atoms. (b) Name the type of force holding the ions together and describe the structure of the solid.
items.answer: (a) 2,1; 2,5 (b) Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; a giant ionic lattice with ions in a regular repeating arrangement.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: electrostatic attraction; 1 mark: giant lattice [2]

items.stem: Isla heats aluminium (proton number 13) in fluorine (proton number 9). A white solid, aluminium fluoride, is formed. (a) Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of the compound, showing outer shells only. (b) Deduce the formula of the compound.
items.answer: (a) 1 Al³⁺ ion(s) with empty/full outer shell and 3 F⁻ ion(s) each with 8 outer electrons (including 1 of the other symbol); brackets and charges. (b) AlF₃
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct number of each ion; 1 mark: 8 electrons on anion with transferred electrons shown; 1 mark: charges [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Ana heats potassium (proton number 19) in oxygen (proton number 8). A white solid, potassium oxide, is formed. (a) Give the electronic configurations of both atoms. (b) Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of the compound, showing outer shells only.
items.answer: (a) 2,8,8,1; 2,6 (b) 2 K⁺ ion(s) with empty/full outer shell and 1 O²⁻ ion(s) each with 8 outer electrons (including 2 of the other symbol); brackets and charges.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: correct number of each ion; 1 mark: 8 electrons on anion with transferred electrons shown; 1 mark: charges [3]

items.stem: Noah heats magnesium (proton number 12) in oxygen (proton number 8). A white solid, magnesium oxide, is formed. (a) Describe how the ions are formed. (b) Deduce the formula of the compound. (c) Predict two physical properties of the compound and explain one of them.
items.answer: (a) magnesium loses 2 electron(s) to form Mg²⁺; oxygen gains 2 to form O²⁻. (b) MgO (c) High melting point (many strong electrostatic forces to overcome); conducts when molten or dissolved (ions free to move), not as a solid.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each ion with electrons lost/gained [2] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark each property; 1 mark explanation [3]

items.stem: Which statement describes the structure of solid sodium chloride?
options: separate NaCl molecules held by weak forces
Na atoms and Cl atoms sharing electrons
a giant lattice of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons
items.answer: a giant lattice of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
items.markingKey: Giant ionic lattice: regular arrangement of oppositely charged ions.

items.stem: Explain why molten sodium chloride conducts electricity but solid sodium chloride does not.
items.answer: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice; when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: solid ions fixed; 1 mark: molten ions mobile / carry charge [2]

items.stem: Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.
items.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges, so the electrostatic attraction between the ions is much stronger than between Na⁺ and Cl⁻; more energy is needed to overcome it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: higher charges on ions; 1 mark: stronger attraction → more energy [2]

items.stem: A substance has these properties: m.p. 3550 °C; conducts when solid: no; conducts when molten: no; solubility: insoluble. What type of structure does it have?
items.answer: giant covalent
items.markingKey: Giant covalent: very high melting point (many strong covalent bonds) and does not conduct (except graphite).

items.stem: The properties of 3 substances are given. W: m.p. 55 °C, conducts when solid: no, conducts when molten/liquid: no, solubility in water: insoluble; X: m.p. 734 °C, conducts when solid: no, conducts when molten/liquid: yes, solubility in water: soluble; solution conducts; Y: m.p. 3550 °C, conducts when solid: no, conducts when molten/liquid: no, solubility in water: insoluble. Deduce the type of structure of each substance, giving a reason for each.
items.answer: W: simple molecular; X: giant ionic; Y: giant covalent
items.markingKey: W simple molecular (low melting point (weak intermolecular forces) and does not conduct in any state (no ions or free electrons)); X giant ionic (high melting point and conducts only when molten or in solution (ions free to move)); Y giant covalent (very high melting point (many strong covalent bonds) and does not conduct (except graphite)). 1 mark per structure with reason [3]

items.stem: Amara tests a sample of potassium bromide, KBr, which melts at 734 °C. (a) Explain why it has a high melting point. (b) Explain why the crystals are brittle.
items.answer: (a) strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice needs much energy to overcome (b) a force shifts layers so like-charged ions meet and repel, so the crystal cracks
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: strong attraction between ions; 1 mark: many / need much energy [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?
options: Its ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move.
items.answer: Its ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move.
items.markingKey: Ions in the lattice cannot move; when molten or dissolved they can.

items.stem: Describe the structure of a giant ionic lattice.
items.answer: A regular three-dimensional repeating arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions, each held by strong electrostatic attraction to the oppositely charged ions around it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: regular 3D arrangement; 1 mark: alternating oppositely charged ions attracted in all directions [2]

items.stem: A substance has these properties: m.p. 660 °C; conducts when solid: yes; conducts when molten: yes; solubility: insoluble. What type of structure does it have?
items.answer: metallic
items.markingKey: Metallic: conducts electricity when solid and when liquid (delocalised electrons).

items.stem: A substance has these properties: m.p. 650 °C; conducts when solid: yes; conducts when molten: yes; solubility: insoluble (reacts slowly). What type of structure does it have?
items.answer: metallic
items.markingKey: Metallic: conducts electricity when solid and when liquid (delocalised electrons).

items.stem: What is a covalent bond?
options: the attraction between oppositely charged ions
the attraction between ions and delocalised electrons
the transfer of electrons from one atom to another
a pair of electrons shared between two atoms
items.answer: a pair of electrons shared between two atoms
items.markingKey: Covalent bond: shared pair of electrons.

items.stem: Explain why boiling water does not break the covalent bonds in water molecules.
items.answer: Boiling only overcomes the weak intermolecular forces between molecules; the strong covalent bonds within each molecule stay intact (steam is still H₂O).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: intermolecular forces overcome; 1 mark: covalent bonds strong / not broken [2]

items.stem: Explain why the boiling point of bromine is higher than that of chlorine.
items.answer: Bromine molecules are larger with a greater relative molecular mass, so the intermolecular forces between them are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: larger Mr / molecules; 1 mark: stronger intermolecular forces [2]

items.stem: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl, showing outer-shell electrons only. State the number of bonding pairs and non-bonding pairs.
items.answer: 1 single bond (1 bonding pairs) and 3 non-bonding pair(s); every atom has a full outer shell (H: 2; others: 8).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: 1 single bond shown as shared pairs (one dot + one cross each); 1 mark: 3 lone pair(s) correctly placed; 1 mark: each atom has full outer shell [3]

items.stem: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of ethene, C₂H₄, showing outer-shell electrons only. State the number of bonding pairs and non-bonding pairs.
items.answer: 4 single bonds and 1 double bond (6 bonding pairs) and 0 non-bonding pair(s); every atom has a full outer shell (H: 2; others: 8).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: 4 single bonds and 1 double bond shown as shared pairs (one dot + one cross each); 1 mark: 0 lone pair(s) correctly placed; 1 mark: each atom has full outer shell [3]

items.stem: Lucas is studying carbon dioxide, CO₂, a simple molecular substance. (a) Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of the molecule (outer shells only). (b) Explain why it does not conduct electricity.
items.answer: (a) 2 double bonds; 4 lone pair(s); full outer shells (b) molecules are neutral; no ions or delocalised electrons
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: bonding pairs; 1 mark: lone pairs; 1 mark: full shells [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: How many electrons are shared in the bond between the two atoms in a nitrogen molecule, N₂?
items.markingKey: N≡N triple bond: 3 shared pairs = 6 electrons.

items.stem: Explain how the atoms in a hydrogen chloride molecule achieve stable electronic configurations.
items.answer: H and Cl each share one electron in a single covalent bond; H then has 2 outer electrons (like He) and Cl has 8 (like Ar).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one shared pair; 1 mark: both achieve full outer shells [2]

items.stem: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of ethane, C₂H₆, showing outer-shell electrons only. State the number of bonding pairs and non-bonding pairs.
items.answer: 7 single bonds (7 bonding pairs) and 0 non-bonding pair(s); every atom has a full outer shell (H: 2; others: 8).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: 7 single bonds shown as shared pairs (one dot + one cross each); 1 mark: 0 lone pair(s) correctly placed; 1 mark: each atom has full outer shell [3]

items.stem: Boiling points of some simple molecular substances: ethanol (C₂H₅OH): 78 °C, propanol (C₃H₇OH): 97 °C. Describe the trend in boiling point with relative molecular mass and explain it.
items.answer: Boiling point increases as Mr increases (C₂H₅OH 46, C₃H₇OH 60): larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Mr values / ordering; 1 mark: b.p. increases with Mr; 1 mark: stronger intermolecular forces need more energy [3]

items.stem: How many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom covalently bonded to in diamond?
items.markingKey: Diamond: tetrahedral, 4 bonds per C.

items.stem: Explain why diamond is hard but graphite is soft, even though both contain only carbon atoms.
items.answer: In diamond each C is bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3D network of strong covalent bonds; graphite has layers held by weak forces that slide over each other.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diamond rigid 3D 4 bonds; 1 mark: graphite layers with weak forces slide [2]

items.stem: Explain why silicon(IV) oxide has a much higher melting point than carbon dioxide, even though both are oxides of Group IV elements.
items.answer: SiO₂ is a giant covalent structure – melting breaks many strong covalent bonds; CO₂ is simple molecular – melting/subliming overcomes only weak intermolecular forces.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: SiO₂ giant covalent, strong bonds broken; 1 mark: CO₂ simple molecules, weak intermolecular forces [2]

items.stem: Three solids are tested. A: m.p. 3652 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes; B: m.p. 801 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; C: m.p. 146 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no. Identify which solid(s) have a giant covalent structure and explain your choice.
items.answer: A: A is giant covalent; B is giant ionic; C is simple molecular
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A; 1 mark: very high m.p. (many strong covalent bonds); 1 mark: does not conduct (or graphite exception) / rules out others [3]

items.stem: Three solids are tested. A: m.p. 1414 °C, conducts as solid: slightly (semiconductor), conducts when molten: yes; B: m.p. 420 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes; C: m.p. 660 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes. Identify which solid(s) have a giant covalent structure and explain your choice.
items.answer: A: A is giant covalent; B is metallic; C is metallic
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A; 1 mark: very high m.p. (many strong covalent bonds); 1 mark: does not conduct (or graphite exception) / rules out others [3]

items.stem: An engineering company in Auckland must choose materials for drill tips, electrodes and furnace linings from diamond, graphite and silicon(IV) oxide. (a) State and explain which substance is used for drill tips. (b) Suggest why graphite is used for electrodes but diamond is not.
items.answer: (a) diamond: very hard because of the rigid 3D network of strong covalent bonds (b) graphite conducts (delocalised electrons); diamond has none
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: diamond; 1 mark: reason [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
items.answer: In graphite each carbon forms 3 bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move; in diamond all 4 outer electrons are in bonds.

items.stem: Describe the structure of silicon(IV) oxide.
items.answer: A giant covalent lattice in which each silicon atom is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom to two silicon atoms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: giant covalent; 1 mark: Si to 4 O and O to 2 Si [2]

items.stem: Three solids are tested. A: m.p. 801 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; B: m.p. 55 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; C: m.p. 1710 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no. Identify which solid(s) have a giant covalent structure and explain your choice.
items.answer: C: A is giant ionic; B is simple molecular; C is giant covalent
items.markingKey: 1 mark: C; 1 mark: very high m.p. (many strong covalent bonds); 1 mark: does not conduct (or graphite exception) / rules out others [3]

items.stem: Three solids are tested. A: m.p. 0 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no (pure); B: m.p. 3550 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; C: m.p. 660 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes. Identify which solid(s) have a giant covalent structure and explain your choice. Suggest the identity of each solid.
items.answer: B: A is simple molecular; B is giant covalent; C is metallic. Identities: A could be water, B could be diamond, C could be aluminium
items.markingKey: 1 mark: B; 1 mark: very high m.p. (many strong covalent bonds); 1 mark: does not conduct (or graphite exception) / rules out others [3]; identities [1]

items.stem: What is metallic bonding?
options: the attraction between positive and negative ions
the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
a weak force between metal molecules
the sharing of a pair of electrons between two metal atoms
items.answer: the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
items.markingKey: Metallic bond: lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.

items.stem: Explain why metals conduct electricity when solid but ionic compounds do not.
items.answer: Metals have delocalised electrons that move through the lattice; in a solid ionic compound the ions are fixed and there are no free electrons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: metal delocalised electrons move; 1 mark: ionic solid ions fixed [2]

items.stem: Describe the structure and bonding in a metal such as magnesium.
items.answer: A giant lattice of Mg²⁺ ions in a regular arrangement surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons (two from each atom); strong electrostatic attraction between the ions and the electrons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lattice of positive ions; 1 mark: delocalised electrons; 1 mark: electrostatic attraction [3]

items.stem: Which substance is a metal? P: m.p. 772 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; Q: m.p. 55 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; R: m.p. 3550 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; S: m.p. 420 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes.
items.answer: S
items.markingKey: S conducts when solid and molten: delocalised electrons → metallic.

items.stem: Data for four substances: P: m.p. 115 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; Q: m.p. 734 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; R: m.p. 3550 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; S: m.p. 420 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes. Identify the metal and explain how the data support your answer. Describe the type of structure of each of the other substances.
items.answer: S is the metal (conducts as solid and liquid – delocalised electrons). P: simple molecular; Q: giant ionic; R: giant covalent
items.markingKey: 1 mark: metal identified; 1 mark: conducts when solid due to delocalised electrons; 1 mark per two other structures correct up to [2] total [4]

items.stem: Sipho investigates why silver is chosen for electrical contacts. (a) Explain why metals conduct electricity. (b) Suggest why the alloy is often harder than the pure metal.
items.answer: (a) delocalised electrons move through the structure when a p.d. is applied (b) different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers so they cannot slide easily

items.stem: Explain why metals usually have high melting points.
items.answer: Strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons throughout the giant lattice requires much energy to overcome.

items.stem: Compare the conduction of electricity by copper and by molten sodium chloride.
items.answer: Copper: delocalised electrons move, no chemical change. Molten NaCl: ions move to the electrodes and are discharged (electrolysis).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: electrons in copper; 1 mark: ions in molten NaCl [2]

items.stem: Data for four substances: P: m.p. 734 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; Q: m.p. 146 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; R: m.p. 1085 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes; S: m.p. 114 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no. Identify the metal and explain how the data support your answer. Describe the type of structure of each of the other substances.
items.answer: R is the metal (conducts as solid and liquid – delocalised electrons). P: giant ionic; Q: simple molecular; S: simple molecular
items.markingKey: 1 mark: metal identified; 1 mark: conducts when solid due to delocalised electrons; 1 mark per two other structures correct up to [2] total [4]

items.stem: An engineer in Hanoi explains to apprentices why copper is used for electrical wiring. (a) Describe the structure and bonding in a metal. (b) Explain why metals have high melting points.
items.answer: (a) giant lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons; electrostatic attraction between them (b) strong attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons needs much energy to overcome
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: positive ions lattice; 1 mark: delocalised electrons; 1 mark: attraction [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Which type of element forms positive ions?
items.answer: metals
items.markingKey: Metal atoms lose outer electrons to form positive ions.

items.stem: A student says, "In sodium chloride, sodium and chlorine share an electron." Explain the error.
items.answer: In ionic bonding electrons are transferred, not shared: sodium loses one electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that attract each other.

items.stem: Describe, in terms of electrons, how sodium chloride forms when sodium reacts with chlorine.
items.answer: Each sodium atom (2,8,1) loses 1 outer electron to form Na⁺ (2,8); each chlorine atom (2,8,7) gains 1 electron to form Cl⁻ (2,8,8). and the oppositely charged ions attract (ionic bond), giving NaCl.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sodium loses 1 electron(s); 1 mark: chlorine gains 1 electron(s); 1 mark: ions Na⁺ and Cl⁻ [3]

items.stem: Describe, in terms of electrons, how potassium oxide forms when potassium reacts with oxygen. Include the electronic configurations of the atoms and ions (proton numbers: potassium 19, oxygen 8).
items.answer: Each potassium atom (2,8,8,1) loses 1 outer electron to form K⁺ (2,8,8); each oxygen atom (2,6) gains 2 electrons to form O²⁻ (2,8). 2 potassium atoms transfer electrons to 1 oxygen atom, and the oppositely charged ions attract (ionic bond), giving K₂O.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: potassium loses 1 electron(s); 1 mark: oxygen gains 2 electron(s); 1 mark: ions K⁺ and O²⁻; 1 mark: configurations 2,8,8,1 → 2,8,8 and 2,6 → 2,8 [4]

items.stem: Aluminium sulfide is an ionic compound formed from aluminium (proton number 13) and sulfur (proton number 16). A research group in Istanbul is studying its structure. (a) Give the electronic configurations of both atoms. (b) Name the type of force holding the ions together and describe the structure of the solid.
items.answer: (a) 2,8,3; 2,8,6 (b) Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; a giant ionic lattice with ions in a regular repeating arrangement.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: electrostatic attraction; 1 mark: giant lattice [2]

items.stem: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
options: There are weak forces between molecules.
There are strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice.
The electrons are free to move.
items.answer: There are strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice.
items.markingKey: Much energy is needed to overcome the many strong ionic bonds.

items.stem: Explain why ionic crystals are brittle and shatter when hit.
items.answer: A force shifts a layer of ions so that ions of the same charge line up next to each other; they repel and the crystal splits.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: layers shift; 1 mark: like charges repel [2]

items.stem: A substance has these properties: m.p. 801 °C; conducts when solid: no; conducts when molten: yes; solubility: soluble; solution conducts. What type of structure does it have?
items.answer: giant ionic
items.markingKey: Giant ionic: high melting point and conducts only when molten or in solution (ions free to move).

items.stem: A ceramics company in Kuala Lumpur uses sodium chloride, NaCl (m.p. 801 °C), in its products. (a) Explain why the crystals are brittle. (b) Suggest why a solution of sodium chloride in water conducts electricity. (c) Name the ions present and give the ratio in which they are present.
items.answer: (a) a force shifts layers so like-charged ions meet and repel, so the crystal cracks (b) the ions separate and are free to move in the solution (c) Na and Cl ions in ratio 1:1

items.stem: How many non-bonding (lone) pairs of outer-shell electrons are there in one molecule of ethane, C₂H₆?
items.markingKey: Outer electrons not used in bonding: 0 lone pair(s).

items.stem: Explain why a nitrogen molecule is described as having a triple bond.
items.answer: Each N atom (2,5) needs three more electrons, so the two atoms share three pairs of electrons.

items.stem: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of water, H₂O, showing outer-shell electrons only. State the number of bonding pairs and non-bonding pairs.
items.answer: 2 single bonds (2 bonding pairs) and 2 non-bonding pair(s); every atom has a full outer shell (H: 2; others: 8).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: 2 single bonds shown as shared pairs (one dot + one cross each); 1 mark: 2 lone pair(s) correctly placed; 1 mark: each atom has full outer shell [3]

items.stem: Sofia is studying methanol, CH₃OH, a simple molecular substance. (a) Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of the molecule (outer shells only). (b) Explain why the substance has a low melting point.
items.answer: (a) 5 single bonds; 2 lone pair(s); full outer shells (b) weak intermolecular forces between molecules are easily overcome (covalent bonds not broken)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: bonding pairs; 1 mark: lone pairs; 1 mark: full shells [3] (b) 1 mark: weak intermolecular forces; 1 mark: little energy needed [2]

items.stem: A student says, "Graphite has a low melting point because its layers slide easily." Explain the error.
items.answer: Melting requires breaking the strong covalent bonds within the layers, so graphite has a very high melting point; the weak forces between layers only explain its softness.

items.stem: A company in Nairobi chooses diamond because it does not conduct electricity. Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why diamond does not conduct electricity.
items.answer: All four outer electrons of each carbon atom are used in covalent bonds, so there are no delocalised electrons or ions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: giant covalent structure; 1 mark: number of bonds per atom / layers; 1 mark: linked to the property [3]

items.stem: Three solids are tested. A: m.p. 1414 °C, conducts as solid: slightly (semiconductor), conducts when molten: yes; B: m.p. 2072 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; C: m.p. 845 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes. Identify which solid(s) have a giant covalent structure and explain your choice.
items.answer: A: A is giant covalent; B is giant ionic; C is giant ionic
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A; 1 mark: very high m.p. (many strong covalent bonds); 1 mark: does not conduct (or graphite exception) / rules out others [3]

items.stem: Nadia compares three substances: diamond, graphite and silicon(IV) oxide. (a) Describe the structure of graphite and explain how it conducts electricity. (b) State and explain which substance is used for drill tips. (c) Explain why silicon(IV) oxide is suitable for lining furnaces.
items.answer: (a) layers of hexagons, each C bonded to 3 others; one delocalised electron per atom moves along the layers (b) diamond: very hard because of the rigid 3D network of strong covalent bonds (c) very high melting point: many strong covalent bonds in a giant structure; also does not react/burn
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: layers / 3 bonds; 1 mark: delocalised electrons move [2] (b) 1 mark: diamond; 1 mark: reason [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: A student says, "Metals conduct electricity because their positive ions move." Explain the error.
items.answer: The positive ions are fixed in the lattice; it is the delocalised electrons that move and carry the current.

items.stem: Which substance is a metal? P: m.p. 772 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; Q: m.p. 420 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes; R: m.p. 734 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; S: m.p. −114 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no.
items.answer: Q
items.markingKey: Q conducts when solid and molten: delocalised electrons → metallic.

items.stem: Data for four substances: P: m.p. 2852 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; Q: m.p. 1414 °C, conducts as solid: slightly (semiconductor), conducts when molten: yes; R: m.p. 801 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; S: m.p. 1085 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes. Identify the metal and explain how the data support your answer. Describe the type of structure of each of the other substances.
items.answer: S is the metal (conducts as solid and liquid – delocalised electrons). P: giant ionic; Q: giant covalent; R: giant ionic
items.markingKey: 1 mark: metal identified; 1 mark: conducts when solid due to delocalised electrons; 1 mark per two other structures correct up to [2] total [4]

items.stem: What is the charge on an ion formed from an atom with the electronic configuration 2,8,7?
items.markingKey: It gains one electron to reach 2,8,8.

items.stem: Explain why ionic bonds form between metals and non-metals but not usually between two non-metals.
items.answer: Metals have few outer electrons and lose them easily; non-metals have nearly full outer shells and gain electrons. Two non-metals both tend to gain electrons, so they share instead.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: metals lose, non-metals gain; 1 mark: two non-metals share (covalent) [2]

items.stem: Leila, a student in Manila, burns magnesium in sulfur to make magnesium sulfide. Describe how the ions form, in terms of electron transfer.
items.answer: Each magnesium atom (2,8,2) loses 2 outer electrons to form Mg²⁺ (2,8); each sulfur atom (2,8,6) gains 2 electrons to form S²⁻ (2,8,8). and the oppositely charged ions attract (ionic bond), giving MgS.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: magnesium loses 2 electron(s); 1 mark: sulfur gains 2 electron(s); 1 mark: ions Mg²⁺ and S²⁻ [3]

items.stem: Hana, a student in Bangkok, burns potassium in chlorine to make potassium chloride. Describe how the ions form, in terms of electron transfer. Include the electronic configurations of the atoms and ions (proton numbers: potassium 19, chlorine 17).
items.answer: Each potassium atom (2,8,8,1) loses 1 outer electron to form K⁺ (2,8,8); each chlorine atom (2,8,7) gains 1 electron to form Cl⁻ (2,8,8). and the oppositely charged ions attract (ionic bond), giving KCl.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: potassium loses 1 electron(s); 1 mark: chlorine gains 1 electron(s); 1 mark: ions K⁺ and Cl⁻; 1 mark: configurations 2,8,8,1 → 2,8,8 and 2,8,7 → 2,8,8 [4]

items.stem: Mateo heats calcium (proton number 20) in nitrogen (proton number 7). A white solid, calcium nitride, is formed. (a) Deduce the formula of the compound. (b) Predict two physical properties of the compound and explain one of them.
items.answer: (a) Ca₃N₂ (b) High melting point (many strong electrostatic forces to overcome); conducts when molten or dissolved (ions free to move), not as a solid.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark each property; 1 mark explanation [3]

items.stem: Which property is typical of an ionic compound?
options: It has a low melting point.
items.answer: It conducts electricity when molten.
items.markingKey: Ions become mobile when molten or aqueous.

items.stem: A student says, "Sodium chloride solution conducts because electrons move through it." Explain the error.
items.answer: In the solution it is the ions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻) that move and carry the charge, not electrons.

items.stem: A substance has these properties: m.p. 734 °C; conducts when solid: no; conducts when molten: yes; solubility: soluble; solution conducts. What type of structure does it have?
items.answer: giant ionic
items.markingKey: Giant ionic: high melting point and conducts only when molten or in solution (ions free to move).

items.stem: A ceramics company in Lisbon uses potassium bromide, KBr (m.p. 734 °C), in its products. (a) Describe and explain its electrical conductivity when solid and when molten. (b) Explain why the crystals are brittle.
items.answer: (a) solid: does not conduct, ions fixed; molten: conducts, ions free to move (b) a force shifts layers so like-charged ions meet and repel, so the crystal cracks
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each state with reason [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: How many non-bonding (lone) pairs of outer-shell electrons are there in one molecule of nitrogen, N₂?
items.markingKey: Outer electrons not used in bonding: 2 lone pair(s).

items.stem: A student says, "Simple molecular substances have low melting points because covalent bonds are weak." Explain the error.
items.answer: Covalent bonds are strong; melting overcomes only the weak intermolecular forces between molecules.

items.stem: Boiling points of some simple molecular substances: propane (C₃H₈): −42 °C, methane (CH₄): −162 °C. Describe the trend in boiling point with relative molecular mass and explain it.
items.answer: Boiling point increases as Mr increases (CH₄ 16, C₃H₈ 44): larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Mr values / ordering; 1 mark: b.p. increases with Mr; 1 mark: stronger intermolecular forces need more energy [3]

items.stem: A chemistry textbook in Singapore uses ethene, C₂H₄, as an example of covalent bonding. (a) State the total number of electrons shared in one molecule. (b) Explain why it does not conduct electricity. (c) Calculate its relative molecular mass. (d) Suggest how its boiling point would compare with a similar substance of much larger Mr, giving a reason.
items.answer: (a) 12 (b) molecules are neutral; no ions or delocalised electrons (c) 28 (d) lower: smaller molecules have weaker intermolecular forces
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) [1] (c) 2 × 12 + 4 × 1 [1] (d) 1 mark: lower; 1 mark: reason [2]

items.stem: Felix reads that diamond is used in the tips of cutting tools and drills. Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why diamond is used in the tips of cutting tools and drills.
items.answer: Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a rigid giant tetrahedral structure; many strong bonds must be broken, so it is very hard.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: structure named / described; 1 mark: bonding linked to the property [2]

items.stem: A company in Seoul chooses silicon(IV) oxide because it is hard and is used in sandpaper. Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why silicon(IV) oxide is hard and is used in sandpaper.
items.answer: A rigid three-dimensional network of strong covalent bonds, similar to diamond.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: giant covalent structure; 1 mark: number of bonds per atom / layers; 1 mark: linked to the property [3]

items.stem: Three solids are tested. A: m.p. 3550 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; B: m.p. 55 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; C: m.p. 420 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes. Identify which solid(s) have a giant covalent structure and explain your choice.
items.answer: A: A is giant covalent; B is simple molecular; C is metallic
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A; 1 mark: very high m.p. (many strong covalent bonds); 1 mark: does not conduct (or graphite exception) / rules out others [3]

items.stem: Hana compares three substances: diamond, graphite and silicon(IV) oxide. (a) Describe the structure of diamond. (b) Describe the structure of graphite and explain how it conducts electricity. (c) Explain why silicon(IV) oxide is suitable for lining furnaces.
items.answer: (a) giant covalent; each C bonded to 4 others tetrahedrally (b) layers of hexagons, each C bonded to 3 others; one delocalised electron per atom moves along the layers (c) very high melting point: many strong covalent bonds in a giant structure; also does not react/burn
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: giant covalent; 1 mark: four bonds per C [2] (b) 1 mark: layers / 3 bonds; 1 mark: delocalised electrons move [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Silver is used for electrical contacts. Give the properties that make it suitable, and explain, using the model of metallic bonding, why metals such as silver has a high melting point.
items.answer: It is the best conductor of electricity. A metal has a high melting point because there is strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons, which needs a lot of energy to overcome.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: property; 1 mark: explanation [2]

items.stem: Which substance is a metal? P: m.p. 660 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes; Q: m.p. 2852 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; R: m.p. 1710 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; S: m.p. −114 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no.
items.answer: P
items.markingKey: P conducts when solid and molten: delocalised electrons → metallic.

items.stem: Data for four substances: P: m.p. 650 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes; Q: m.p. 55 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; R: m.p. 2852 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; S: m.p. 845 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes. Identify the metal and explain how the data support your answer. Describe the type of structure of each of the other substances.
items.answer: P is the metal (conducts as solid and liquid – delocalised electrons). Q: simple molecular; R: giant ionic; S: giant ionic
items.markingKey: 1 mark: metal identified; 1 mark: conducts when solid due to delocalised electrons; 1 mark per two other structures correct up to [2] total [4]
